title: $\texttt{Multi}^2$: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Decision-Making with LLM-Based Agents in Interactive Environments
claim: Baselines degrade sharply as task horizon grows and consume more tokens per unit performance; ours stays robust and efficient.
layout: 2 panels side by side: line plot left, bar chart right, ours highlighted
description: Two side-by-side plots compare three methods: ReAct, Glider and the proposed method. Panel (a), titled Horizon Robustness, is a line chart of performance in percent against horizon length (short, medium, long). The proposed method is a bold dark slate-blue line with circle markers. It stays near 70 and dips slightly at long horizons. Glider is a light gray solid line that falls from about 68 to about 49. ReAct is a dashed pale gray line that falls from about 33 to about 12. A legend sits at lower left. Panel (b), titled Token Efficiency, is a bar chart of normalized token efficiency. ReAct is about 0.22 with a dashed outline, Glider is about 0.75, and the proposed method is 1.0 in light blue. Color emphasis is on the proposed method, with the baselines muted in gray.
caption: Challenges in long-horizon interaction on the Science- World using Llama-3.1 8B backbone. We compare ReAct [14] (prompt-based, non-hierarchical), Glider [15] (hierarchical finetuning baseline), and our method (Multi2). (a) Horizon Robustness: performance as a function of horizon length, where longer horizons induce larger degradation for baselines. (b) Token Ef- ficiency: normalized inference-time token efficiency (higher is better), computed as performance/tokens and normalized such that the proposed method equals 1.0.
abstract: A central goal of large language model (LLM) research is to build agentic systems that can plan, act, and adapt through sustained interaction with dynamic environments. While recent LLM-based agents exhibit impressive contextual reasoning, their long-horizon decision-making remains fragile, often suffering from objective drift, where goals and plans drift over extended interactions. We introduce Multi$^2$, a hierarchical multi-agent decision-making framework that explicitly decomposes agent behavior into complementary roles. A high-level agent (System 1) focuses on context-aware sub-goal generation using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while a low-level agent (System 2) executes atomic actions through offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) in interactive environments. This separation enables stable long-horizon control, mitigates objective drift, and allows efficient adaptation. Across diverse interactive environments, Multi$^2$ consistently outperforms strong agentic baselines, demonstrating improved robustness and coordination in multi-turn interaction. Beyond performance, we introduce and release three hierarchical benchmark datasets, filling a long-standing gap in training and evaluating hierarchical decision-making for LLM-based agents.
